title: Find all duplicates in an array (index-marking or frequency map).
shortTitle: Find All Duplicates in an Array — Index-Marking or Frequency Map
topicTitle: Maximum Subarray / Kadane's Algorithm — running sum, reset w

s1_definition.profdef: Finding all duplicates reports every value that appears more than once in an array. A general solution uses a frequency map counting occurrences and collecting keys seen at least twice, running in linear time with linear extra space. A space-optimized solution, valid only when values are in the range one to the array length, marks each visited index by negating the element at the position encoded by the value, and a value whose target slot is already negative is a duplicate, achieving linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India processes a batch of transaction reference numbers and the fraud team must spot every reference that appears more than once, since duplicates can mean a double-charge. The simple way is a tally sheet, one tick per reference, and report any with two or more ticks. A clever space-free way, when the references are numbered one to batch-size, is to flip a mark at the slot each reference points to, and if that slot is already flipped, the reference is a repeat.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count with a frequency map, or when values are one to n, flip the sign at the indexed slot and a pre-flipped slot means a duplicate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding all duplicates reports every value that appears more than once in an array. A general solution uses a frequency map counting occurrences and collecting keys seen at least twice, running in linear time with linear extra space. A space-optimized solution, valid only when values are in the range one to the array length, marks each visited index by negating the element at the position encoded by the value, and a value whose target slot is already negative is a duplicate, achieving linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India processes a batch of transaction reference numbers and the fraud team must spot every reference that appears more than once, since duplicates can mean a double-charge. The simple way is a tally sheet, one tick per reference, and report any with two or more ticks. A clever space-free way, when the references are numbered one to batch-size, is to flip a mark at the slot each reference points to, and if that slot is already flipped, the reference is a repeat.

**One line to remember:** Count with a frequency map, or when values are one to n, flip the sign at the indexed slot and a pre-flipped slot means a duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
The general and always-safe approach is a frequency map, a HashMap from value to count. You walk the array once, incrementing each value's count, and then collect every value whose count is at least two, or you collect a value the moment its count reaches exactly two to avoid reporting it multiple times. This is linear time and linear extra space and works for any values, negative, large, or sparse.

The space-optimized index-marking approach works only under a specific constraint: every value is in the range one to the length of the array, and you are allowed to mutate the array. The idea is to use the array itself as the tally sheet. For each value v you read, you compute the target index as the absolute value of v minus one, because values are one-based and indices are zero-based. You look at the element currently at that target index. If it is already negative, that means some earlier value already pointed here, so v is a duplicate and you record it. Otherwise you negate the element at the target index to mark that v has been seen. Using the absolute value when computing the index is essential because the element you read may itself have been negated earlier.

The reason index-marking achieves constant extra space is that it stores the seen-or-not information inside the sign bit of the array's own elements, so no separate structure is needed. It is a classic trick that interviewers use to test whether you can exploit a tight value-range constraint rather than reaching for a map by reflex.

A senior point is restoring the array. Negating elements mutates the input, which may be unacceptable if the caller needs the original values. If restoration is required, after collecting duplicates you walk the array again and take the absolute value of every element to undo the marks. I mention this trade-off explicitly because silently corrupting a caller's data is a real bug in production.

Another senior point is choosing between the two approaches. If the value range constraint does not hold, or mutation is forbidden, I use the frequency map. If the constraint holds and memory is tight, such as processing huge batches, index-marking saves the linear extra space. For reference identifiers I treat them as the one-to-n indices directly; for arbitrary amounts I use the map keyed by BigDecimal.

A small finance-domain example with the map: `Map<String,Integer> freq=new HashMap<>(); for(String ref:refs){ if(freq.merge(ref,1,Integer::sum)==2) dups.add(ref); }` collects each duplicated reference exactly once.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives daily batches of transaction reference numbers, and the fraud team must find every reference that appears more than once, because a repeat can indicate an accidental double-charge to Rajesh or Priya. The batches are large, so the detection must be linear. Finding all duplicates is exactly this.

This is exactly how duplicate detection works in Java — either a frequency map tallying each reference, or, when references are numbered one to batch-size, index-marking that flips a sign at the indexed slot.

Problem 2 — When references happen to be numbered one to batch-size the team wants the memory-free index-marking variant, but the original batch must be restored afterward so downstream systems see untouched data. This shows the value-range optimization and the restore-the-array responsibility.

What the code will do: a `DuplicateFinder` with `findDuplicatesByMap(List<String> refs)` for the general case and `findDuplicatesByMarking(int[] ids)` for the one-to-n case that restores the array. The demo detects repeated references in a batch.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data for the map case: references `TXF-01, TXF-02, TXF-01, TXF-03, TXF-02`. For the marking case: ids `4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1`.

Step 1 (map): we walk the references and tally. `TXF-01` goes to count one, `TXF-02` to count one, then `TXF-01` reaches count two so we record it, `TXF-03` to count one, then `TXF-02` reaches count two so we record it. The duplicates are `TXF-01` and `TXF-02`, each reported exactly once because we add only at the moment the count hits two.

Step 2 (marking): value `4` points to index three; that slot holds `7`, positive, so we flip it to `-7`. Value `3` points to index two holding `2`, flip to `-2`. Value `2` points to index one holding `3`, flip to `-3`.

Step 3 (marking): value `7` points to index six holding `3`, flip to `-3`. Value `8` points to index seven holding `1`, flip to `-1`. Now value `2` again points to index one, which already holds `-3`, negative, so `2` is a duplicate and we record it.

Step 4 (marking): value `3`, read as absolute value since the slot may be negative, points to index two holding `-2`, already negative, so `3` is a duplicate and we record it. Value `1` points to index zero holding `4`, positive, flip to `-4`.

Step 5 (marking): the duplicates collected are `2` and `3`. Finally we walk the array once more taking absolute values, restoring it to `4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1`, so downstream systems see the untouched batch.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T19:20:00Z INFO Map duplicates = [TXF-01, TXF-02]
2026-10-26T19:20:00Z INFO Marking duplicates = [2, 3]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Map case: refs → HashMap<ref,count> → collect when count hits 2
    │ TXF-01:1 TXF-02:1 TXF-01:2* TXF-03:1 TXF-02:2*
    ▼
  dups = [TXF-01, TXF-02]

  Marking case: ids[4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1], idx=|v|-1
    │ 4→idx3 flip ; 3→idx2 flip ; 2→idx1 flip
    │ 7→idx6 flip ; 8→idx7 flip ; 2→idx1 already<0 → dup 2
    │ 3→idx2 already<0 → dup 3 ; 1→idx0 flip
    ▼
  restore |values| ; dups = [2, 3]
    ▼
  Output: every repeated reference
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding all duplicates reports every value that appears more than once, and I pick one of two approaches depending on the constraints. The general, always-safe approach is a frequency map: I walk the array once, increment each value's count, and collect a value the instant its count reaches exactly two, so each duplicate is reported once. That is linear time and linear space and works for any values.

When the problem guarantees every value lies in the range one to the array length and allows mutation, I use index-marking to drop the extra space to constant. For each value I compute a target index as the absolute value of the value minus one, and I check the element there: if it is already negative, an earlier value pointed here so this is a duplicate, otherwise I negate it to mark it seen. Reading the absolute value is essential because the element I inspect may itself have been negated earlier. The trick stores the seen flag inside the sign bit of the array's own elements.

The responsibility I always call out is restoring the array. Negating mutates the caller's input, so if the original values are needed afterward I walk the array again and take absolute values to undo the marks, because silently corrupting a caller's data is a real production bug. I also explain when to choose which: map when the range constraint fails or mutation is forbidden, marking when the constraint holds and memory is tight.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in fraud detection to flag every transaction reference that appeared more than once in a daily batch, which can signal a double-charge, using the map for arbitrary reference strings and the memory-free marking variant for batches numbered one to size, restoring the batch for downstream systems. Explaining both approaches, the absolute-value detail, and the restore step shows the interviewer I can match the technique to the constraints rather than reflexively reaching for a map.
